content.title: Embracing the Flipside
content.description: A Personal Reflection on Fostering Compassion, Communication and Celebrating Failures in Leadership
content.author: Dr Asad I Mian

content.text: 'Tabeer' is an Urdu word that means 'interpretation' or 'meaning,' often used in the context of dreams.

As we embarked on the Tabeer initiative, a landmark program crafted to mold the next generation of leaders of the Institute of Business Administration (IBA) through the core values of Compassion, Communication, and Creative Leadership, I found myself deeply immersed in a dream like journey that was as much a discovery for myself as it was for the participants. It occurred to me that Tabeer was powerfully symbolic: the program's aim was to unlock or interpret the potential, meaning, and purpose in future leaders, guiding them to a deeper understanding of their capabilities, values, and the impact they can have through leadership.

This initiative, a joint venture between IBA and Synapse, stands as a testament to the collaborative spirit and visionary zeal of individuals who believe in the transformative power of leadership. Dr. Ayesha Mian - formerly an Associate Professor and Chair of Psychiatry at Aga Khan University (AKU) -  as the Founder and CEO of Synapse Pakistan Neuroscience Institute, and her profound expertise in behavioral science, played a pivotal role in this endeavor. Her insights into the neuroscience of leadership dynamics have been instrumental in setting a solid foundation for the program. With her intrepid team members, the primary purpose of this initiative has been to promote tolerance, celebrate opposing viewpoints, upend the status quo, and ultimately change the way we view differences.

My own journey, as a Professor and past Chair of the Department of Emergency Medicine and Director of the Critical Creative Innovative Thinking (CCIT) Forum at AKU, has always been about exploring the intersections of healthcare innovation and leadership. With our book 'Medjack' and my active engagement in innovation and business incubation, I aimed to offer IBA participants a practical model to understand and harness the power of failure in cultivating forward-thinking solutions. My article in Dawn on celebrating failure was an attempt to articulate a nuanced perspective on failure, not just as an inevitable part of the innovation journey but as a milestone worth celebrating.

The richness of the Tabeer initiative was significantly enhanced by the contributions of Unjela Kaleem, Principal of International Development and Humanitarian Assistance at Miyamoto International. As the keynote speaker, Unjela brought a profound depth of knowledge in storytelling and strategic communications, underscoring the importance of these skills in effective leadership. Her address illuminated the vital role of storytelling in navigating leadership challenges, showcasing how strategic communications can be leveraged to craft compelling narratives of resilience and success. Unjela's insights provided participants with essential tools for leadership in diverse settings, further enriching the Tabeer experience.

Junaid Zuberi, an IBA alumnus and CEO of NAPA, brought his practical experiences in leadership and organizational management to the table. His participation in the panel session on "Celebrating Failure in Leadership," alongside me, under the moderation of Dr. Ayesha Mian, offered a bridge between theoretical concepts and real-world application. The wisdom shared during this session illuminated the multifaceted nature of failure, advocating for a culture where risks are encouraged, and failures are seen as indispensable lessons rather than setbacks.

The evolution of our discussion from embracing to celebrating failure marked a significant journey. Initially, the concept of embracing failure seemed a natural starting point, acknowledging our vulnerabilities and learning from our mistakes. However, as the conversation deepened, we collectively ventured into the realm of celebrating failure. This shift in perspective underscored a deeper understanding of failure as not just an obstacle but a catalyst for growth, innovation, and resilience in 21st century organizational leadership.

A critical component of this transformative experience was the active engagement of IBA students and faculty. The enthusiasm and spirit of inquiry they brought to the sessions were inspiring. Four teams of students had the opportunity to pitch their ideas, applying the principles we discussed to real-world scenarios. The formative feedback provided by the panelists was not just evaluative but also constructive, offering insights that further refined the students' approaches to leadership and innovation.

Reflecting on the Tabeer initiative, it is evident that the collective efforts of Dr. Ayesha Mian, Unjela Kaleem, Junaid Zuberi, and myself have created an exciting platform for exploring contemporary leadership dynamics.

The Creative Leadership initiative is even more relevant to institutions of higher education delving into health sciences such as AKU. I believe students of medicine, nursing, education, humanities, arts, and social sciences, representing the different 'schools' of AKU will benefit from Tabeer like platforms. By placing a strong emphasis on Compassion, Communication, and Creative Leadership, and adopting a progressive stance on failure, we can prepare our students for leadership paths that not only embrace but celebrate failures as essential to personal and professional growth.
